To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Inflammation‐inducible hyperexcitability is a common property of nociceptive DRG neurones innervating the GI tract and is mediated, at least in part, by the modulation of voltage‐gained ion channels.

(a) inflammatory mediators induce hyperexcitability in nociceptive DRG neurons; (b) the hyperexcitability involves changes in voltage‐dependent Na+, K+ and Ca2+ currents and the expression of specific channel subtypes; (c) the changes in channel expression and activity are mediated by specific intracellular pathways; (d) the changes are specific to nociceptive neurons; (e) the changes are reversible; (f) these changes in channel expression/activity

inflammatory mediators modulate the intrinsic properties of visceral sensory neurones and that this hyperexcitability may play an important role in the generation of visceral hyperalgesic states and abdominal pain.

the mechanisms underlying the generation of visceral pain.
understanding the mechanisms of visceral pain and developing novel therapies for the treatment of chronic visceral pain.
the role of voltage-gated ion channels in the modulation of nociceptive neuronal function.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are trying to understand how the nervous system is involved in the development and maintenance of visceral hyperalgesic states.
we have shown that inflammation‐induced hyperalgesia in the gut is due to changes in intrinsic properties of DRG neurones.

inflammation‐induced hyperalgesia is a consequence of a change in the intrinsic properties of DRG neurones, and that this hyperexcitability is mediated by a complex interplay of voltage‐gained ion channels and second messenger pathways, which can be targeted to develop novel analgesics for the treatment of visceral pain.
The main takeaway from our work is that

inflammation-induced changes to voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels in nociceptive dorsal-root-ganglion neurons are key to the development of visceral hyperalgesic states, which are a hallmark of chronic abdominal pain.
the inflammatory response is an essential component in the genesis of visceral hyperalgesic states.
the inflammatory milieu of the GI tract can induce changes in the intrinsic properties of DRG neurones that innervate the bowel and these changes can be targeted to reduce visceral pain.
